speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: With this comes several competing considerations that we need to balance.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: On the one hand, for survival and to keep relevant, Singapore has to continually invest in next bound infrastructure and our people.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: When others look at 5G, we must look at 6G and when others look at Web 3.0, we must imagine Web 4.0.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Our people must have the skills and versatility to take advantage of the new opportunities.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: There are other considerations as well – how to leverage digital solutions on a larger scale to solve real problems yet guarding against cyberattacks, how to incentivise businesses to go digital and, in doing so, how to ensure accountability without making the process so cumbersome that businesses "lose steam".

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: These are not necessarily mutually exclusive, but they require careful balancing and calibration.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: But the only mode of application was through the e‐service and thus requires Singpass.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: For the digitally‐savvy, this would be fuss free and save time.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: But she has no mobile phone or Singpass.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Eventually, her daughter managed to apply for Singpass and linked it to her daughter's phone.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: What if my elderly resident was a single elderly?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: What will the Government do to protect our people, young and old, and businesses – small and big, from new threats that emerge from this fast-evolving space?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: As technology advances rapidly and new solutions with new use cases emerge, existing regulations need to evolve, or new ones have to be formulated.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: But timeliness and finding the sweet spot seem to be challenging.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: These are high‐risk and speculative and often seen as a tool for illicit activities.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Hence, sufficient research and deliberation are needed before formal regulations and policies can be introduced.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: But meanwhile, will we risk becoming too slow and lose potential opportunities?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: With metaverse fast becoming a thing, will our policies and regulations be fast enough to capitalise on its development while addressing transactions, personal data and user interaction issues?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In encouraging enterprises or individuals to digitalise or upskill through monetary incentives, might the process be so tedious such that they decide to remain in their comfort zones and stick to just being good enough and avoid digital transformation altogether?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Hence, I would like to ask how will the Government ensure regulatory changes keep pace with tech advancement.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: How do we ensure that we provide sufficient guardrails, yet not suffocate innovation?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Chairman, do I continue with my next cut?

speaker: The Chairman
text: You can carry on with your second cut.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: Reports of precious lives lost to "bullycides" and life savings lost to online scams are aplenty.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: While nobody is immune, children, youths, women and elderly are especially vulnerable to online harms.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: Years ago, my resident's fiancée was a victim of "revenge porn".

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: Her ex‐boyfriend uploaded intimate material onto websites such as Revenge Porn, attracting unsavoury comments from people she knew and did not know.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: In general, women and girls tend to be victims of body shaming and hyper-sexualisation online.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: In 2020, an elderly resident fell prey to an online investment scam.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: He was misled to believe that the scheme was endorsed by Senior Minister Tharman Shanmugaratnam, which is, of course, not true.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: Due to his lack of knowledge, he gave his one-time password (OTP) away and racked up a huge credit card debt that he could not afford.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: While adults having gone through a few hard knocks in life can arguably cope better, youths and children are still in their innocence and need a lot more protection.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: Online harms cause distress and have long-term adverse consequences in real life.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: We must protect our people from such harms, so that they can live freely and fulfill their potential.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Chairman, the onslaught of online scams, the prevalence of fake websites and the ubiquity of misinformation on social media are having a severe detrimental impact on our society.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The loss of hard-earned money, loss of trust in official and traditional sources of information and the confusion and harm caused by false information interferes with how a nation can function and operate normally and damages our social fabric.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The digital universe has no border and invaders can potentially enter from anywhere if we do not put up our defences.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It is not easy for the man in the street to keep abreast of the latest online scams and newly-evolved digital deceptions.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: What measures does MCI have in place to help protect our people from online harm?

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Chairman, Singaporeans are now spending more time online, which means they are more open to online content – and some content may hold extreme or even extremist views – online gaming and possible gambling as well as engaging in social media that may not be able to regulate all of its contents.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Different segments of the community may be exposed to varied levels of online harms.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: The youths, for example, are most susceptible to negative influences like cyberbullying, hate comments or even online shaming.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Mr Chairman, digitalisation is a priority for many countries, Singapore included.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: However, as mentioned, with increased digitalisation comes exposure to online harms.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Another type relates to content found online, for example, online sexual grooming, doxing, cyberbullying, online harassment or stalking and the sharing of misinformation or unlawful content.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: As we know, platforms, such as OnlyFans, have been used to show unlawful content.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: On the metaverse, there have been reports of avatars being bullied and verbally and sexually harassed virtually.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: I must commend the Ministry for doing much in educating the public on how to navigate the Internet safely.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: However, what can we do to always make sure that we keep ahead of all the online changes and can we do more in terms of regulations?

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: I watch with interest the developments of the Online Safety Bill in the UK which would determine how online platforms should deal with content and how to prevent the propagation of illegal content.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Would the Ministry consider introducing legislation to regulate online content here as well?

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Christopher de Souza, you can take both your cuts.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Mr Chairman, Sir, for SMEs, in particular, while the reality of digitalisation as the future is acknowledged, there is much practical difficulty in terms of initial costs, lack of technical expertise and assisting employees in making that transition, particularly senior employees who have worked for years within the existing system.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: As we prepare for a post-pandemic future, technology can revolutionise and reinvent much of the way business is done.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: With hyperscale cloud providers dominating the cloud infrastructure and more industry clouds appearing, cloud computing has transformed in a way that has changed digitalisation.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Other technologies, such as quantum computing, the metaverse and digital currencies, are continuing to take over the landscape and seemingly unlock more potential.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: How can the Government take advantage of the potential of new digital technologies and invest into it, while at the same time, watching against any potential pitfalls?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This then, can enhance Singapore's competitiveness and resilience.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Mr Chairman, for Singapore to pioneer the model for a globally competitive digital metropolis, the digital space must be economically vibrant, socially stable and digitally secure for all.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Larger businesses tend to have the resources to protect their interests in this digital space.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: How will MCI ensure that the interests of consumers and small businesses continue to be protected in this digital age?

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: (In Mandarin):   During the pre-COVID-19 days, I used to visit Mediacorp once a month to give law awareness radio talk shows on Capital 95.8FM.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: During the intervals, I would sit at a corner and listen to the senior radio news presenter presenting dialect news, like in Hokkien or Cantonese.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: These presenters are usually over 50 years old; occasionally, they would stay behind to wait for me to finish my talk show to have a chat with me in Mandarin or Hokkien, sometimes about getting some legal advice on estate planning.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I have always enjoyed these sessions as they bring back childhood memories of chatting with my Ah Ma.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Like her, most of the seniors only know how to communicate with people in dialects and rely on the vernacular radio news broadcasts to stay updated on current affairs.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Recently, in my catch-up with one of the DJs, I came to understand that due to the COVID-19 situation, these dialect news presenters are now required to record their radio news broadcasts from home.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It has been a challenging time; some of them have sadly passed away, while some have chosen to retire as they found themselves unable to keep up with technology.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: How will the Ministry ensure that radio stations continue to train and retain talents in this aspect in order to continue on with this feature?

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In my capacity as the Advisor to Singapore Union of Broadcasting Employees (SUBE), I also hope that more welfare support can be given to taking care of these dialect news radio presenters.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: (In English): My next cut is on whether a collaboration with Mediacorp will be explored to introduce a cartoon series using rhythmic content akin to Baby Shark or CoComelon YouTube channel songs involving mascots like Captain Green, Water Wally to attract and educate young audiences to become our young budding green champions.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Since we are raising a lot of taxes in this Budget, we should be careful about such a new and big outflow of taxpayers' money.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Do we have an exit plan, or will we keep funding SPH Media Trust for many more years beyond the first five years?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: SPH assets have grown over the years, thanks to the hefty profits of the near-monopoly media business it previously enjoyed.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Although in recent years the print business has become a loss-making business due to the Internet, SPH has maintained overall profitability because of its huge property portfolio.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Can the Minister explain what is the rationale behind the Government's acceptance of such a deal?

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Chairman, as we move towards a digitally-inclusive society, we will not only need to focus on promoting digital literacy and skills, but also on supporting all businesses, especially small and medium‐sized enterprises, and all individuals to guard against both cyber and data threats.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: This will strengthen our collective defences and resilience against bad actors and preserve overall confidence in our digital future.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: In this regard, what plans does MCI have to support our businesses and citizens?

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Advanced digital infrastructure and cybersecurity technologies are important, but we also need to enhance our fundamentals.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: To get a Data Protection Trust Mark (DPTM), there are five assessment bodies with IMDA which can assess an organisation.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: In practice, we do not need every organisation to be certified.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: But, in parallel, we must enhance our understanding of basic data protection law and emphasise the importance of critical data protection requirements.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: How are data protection consultancies regulated in Singapore today?

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: How do we ensure that our data protection ecosystem has the competencies and subject matter experts required to be secure?

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: How can we better build and accelerate our efforts to build trusted, secure and resilient digital infrastructure and technologies?

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: How can we better support businesses and individuals to guard against cyber and data threats?

speaker: Ms Hany Soh
text: With the growing cyber and data threats, how will MCI better protect individuals and businesses and guard against these risks, helping to ensure that they remain confident enough to continue thriving in the digital realm?

speaker: Ms Hany Soh
text: Are there any grants that can be provided to encourage companies to adopt approved cybersecurity solutions that can help these businesses?

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: Mr Chairman, our society and lives are being transformed.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: We use digital technologies every day, whether in a lived, work or play environment.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: We spend so much more time in the online space.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: Hence, we recommended those without a laptop to use the facilities in our national libraries.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: In the past, people go to the libraries to borrow books or to read newspapers and magazines.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: In today's world, reading or acquiring knowledge and information is no longer restricted to the physical print version.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: Sadly, the falling rate of reading is a global trend.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: In this respect, the role of our libraries needs to evolve.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: They could play an indispensable role in supporting Singaporeans to navigate this digital world while cultivating a spirit of lifelong learning and bringing the community together.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: In the past, library users must first be able to read.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: Otherwise, the library collection is useless to them.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: Today, digital literacy is as important as knowing our ABCs.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: So, how will MCI ensure that the benefits of digitalisation extend to all segments of our society?

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: What measures are in place to bridge skills and knowledge gaps and ensure that individuals have the know-how, confidence and motivation to use digital technology?

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: In the late 1990s, our libraries were transformed from functional spaces with rows of bookshelves to vibrant community nodes, where the young and old explore wonders of the written word.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: How are our libraries being refreshed to meet the changing needs and interests of Singaporeans and continue to nurture a love of reading, learning and discovery?

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: I see SG Digital Office ambassadors in the neighbourhood teaching our seniors how to use their smart phones and encouraging heartland shops to come on board and accept digital CDC Vouchers.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: The deployment of resources on the ground has been effective, but how sustainable is it?

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: How can we tap on the diversity, insights and capabilities of the wider community and empower ground-up efforts?

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: Let us do more to welcome more immigrants to the digital world and integrate them well to be truly digital citizens.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Mr Chairman, with digitalisation becoming more pervasive and an integral part of our society, how is the Ministry working with the private and people sectors to bring digital to life for Singaporeans and prepare them for the digital future?

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Today there is a growing need to pay attention to the livelihood aspect of the digital economy which offers some of the most exciting and high-quality jobs across the different sectors.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Under the Smart Nation strategy, we have outlined our ambitions to build a digital economy, a digital Government and a digital society.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Can the Minister let us know the progress of this initiative, especially in terms of the whole-of-nation digitalisation effort?

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Second, Singapore had outlined funding and aims to develop high-tech digital solutions for industry, including being a lab for deploying new technology solutions.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Can the Minister let us know how we are doing in terms of translating novel technologies into commercial products and services?

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Last, part of Singapore's advantage has always been our ability to work across disciplines.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Such innovative inter-disciplinary technology solutions give us the power to address complex challenges.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: It also allows us a special position as a trusted digital innovation hub.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Can the Minister give us an idea how Singapore is doing in terms of its ambition to become as honest agent in digital trust?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha
text: Chairman, in the last two years, we see the accelerated adoption of digital practices in our society.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha
text: Businesses and individuals have transformed quickly to adopt digital solutions.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha
text: However, there are still some Singaporeans and businesses that have not been able to adopt digital solutions.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha
text: How is MCI supporting Singaporeans who are less digitally savvy and have not embraced digital and benefit from its use in their daily lives?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha
text: What more can we do to bring them onboard?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha
text: For our youths, how do we ensure that the gap between the digital "haves" and the digital "have-nots" do not widen?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha
text: What more can we do to support our less privileged youths?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha
text: How can we ensure all youths have access to digital devices, connectivity and the required skillsets so that they are better prepared for the digital economy?

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Tanjong Pagar)
text: On average, Singaporeans own 3.3 connected devices per person.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Amongst us, 91% own a smartphone, sometimes two, and our broadband Internet speed is amongst the highest in Asia.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Couple these trends that have been gathering pace since the 1990s with changes in our lifestyle due to the pandemic in the past two years – work-from-home, home-based learning arrangements, safe management measures, all those have meant that the human connection that each of us yearn for could often only be achieved through technology-mediated means.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Simply put, we cannot live without being digitally connected today.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Technology can either be a boon or a bane through social networking sites, people all over the world can reconnect with long-lost friends, share tips on niche hobbies and rally like-minded individuals passionate about various social causes.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In the same vein, however, these platforms have also allowed terrorist cells from remote corners of the world to link up.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Much, therefore, depends on factors, such as the purpose that technologies are harnessed for and the motivations of individual tech users, amongst others.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Seventy cases were new and many were youths in their 20s.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In many cases, first encounters with sexually explicit materials online start off quite innocuously as a curious conversation between peers or a chance encounter with a sexually explicit site due to random pop-up advertisements.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Tanjong Pagar)
text: But in Asian societies like ours, where parents tend to avoid awkward conversations on such sensitive topics, young impressionable minds are often left on their own to make sense of the material that they come into contact with.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Tanjong Pagar)
text: While many do not find themselves mired in addiction, the fact remains, some do.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Especially when the consumption of sexually explicit material serves as a stress management mechanism.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The question then is: do we know this often invisible issue well enough to design appropriate interventions?

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Gaming itself is not necessarily a bad activity.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It can be a good source of entertainment, stress relief or even character building.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Tanjong Pagar)
text: But things can go south with a small group of gamers when excessive online gaming interferes with one's routines.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Relationships with family and friends can become strained and when gaming becomes a compulsion, one becomes restless and irritable when access to gaming is curbed.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We all reeled in shock here in Singapore when we learnt that a teenager with a gaming addiction killed his father, partly because the father had limited his access to his games.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The related issue is that of in-game loot boxes or "virtual goodie bags with random rewards" as The Straits Times called it.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Of course, this means that prizes are extremely coveted.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Tanjong Pagar)
text: But what is concerning is how addictive loot boxes can become.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Experts have warned that the allure of these loot boxes lie exactly in the excitement of not knowing what one is going to get, much like what Forrest Gump says in the box of chocolates.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This stimulates the production of dopamine, a mood-lifting biochemical typically produced when we exercise, get sufficient sleep or meditate.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Tanjong Pagar)
text: But this keeps the gamer coming back for more.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I have talked about my concerns on sexually explicit materials and gaming.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Tanjong Pagar)
text: But there remain many other issues that needs working through – cyberbullying, misinformation and disinformation, extremism – amongst many others.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I stress again for the record here that I am not making a case against the Internet or gaming or any online platforms.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Tanjong Pagar)
text: But, while I had scratched the surface in terms of these online deals we need to tackle, what is the Ministry's strategy in mobilising resources, channelling societies attention to developing issues?

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Tanjong Pagar)
text: And what are the conversations we need to have as a society?

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Tanjong Pagar)
text: How can we all do our part to make the online world – which actually can be a constructive space for networking, knowledge sharing and content creation – one that is safer for everyone?

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Essentially, the launch of AfA is underpinned by the desire to combat online harms, especially those targeted at women and girls.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Importantly, MCI underscores that the AfA would focus on closing the digital safety gap and on taking actions to enhance the freedom and safety of our women and girls in the digital future.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: As such, the AfA will adopt a whole-of-nation approach to close the digital safety gaps.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Ms Hany Soh, you can take both cuts together.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh
text: How does MCI bridge the digital skills and knowledge gap among Singaporeans and encourage them to seek out digital opportunities to pursue lifelong learning and enrich their lives?

speaker: Ms Hany Soh
text: Apart from the assistance provided by our digital ambassadors, can we consider providing more support to IHLs for the latter to conduct more digital technology training courses for the public?

speaker: Ms Hany Soh
text: It can either be run in a manner similar to SkillsFuture courses or a collaboration with the People's Association whereby IHLs' lecturers and students reach out to vulnerable groups in the community through the residents' community centres, senior activity centres, in order to run these courses.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh
text: During this pandemic period, many of our little ones seek comfort in reading, keeping themselves occupied while their parents are busy with online zoom conferences.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh
text: Besides being a healthy form of entertainment, it can also be a form of bonding as it helps the children to return to their roots by learning traditional stories and rhymes.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh
text: What are the ongoing and upcoming efforts to increase the availability and variety of books and e-resources in Chinese, Malay and Tamil so as to encourage our young readers to master their mother tongue languages?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Mr Chairman, libraries play a special role in igniting the joy of reading and nurturing curiosity and enquiring minds.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The ability to read is fundamental to enable access to information and encouraging lifelong learning in the young and old.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Reading helps develop imagination, creativity, speaking and communication skills.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: My residents, young and old, shared with me their fondness and desire for a library in our estate.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: With the pervasiveness of digitalisation, digital literacy is as important as reading for access to information and lifelong learning.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Our network of public libraries has continued to innovate and transform to stay relevant, including offering digital services.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: How is MCI leveraging our libraries to encourage a self-directed learning culture and spark curiosity among the public to improve their proficiency in digital skills and literacy?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: While digital access allows access to content and programmes, beyond that, the physical libraries do provide community and social spaces for people to come together to learn.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: A highlight of National Library Board's (NLB) LAB25 are installations called Nodes, to serve as new entry points into NLB's wide array of content.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Will NLB consider the installation of Nodes in estates like Simei that do not have a library?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Actually, given the important role that libraries play, it would be even better to have a library in Simei.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Can we have an update of how many businesses have participated and utilised these initiatives?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: And how will they build on and complement the current initiatives?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Apart from these initiatives, I urge MCI and related agencies to consider nurturing "communities of learning and practice" for digital and tech talent.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I believe that this will catalyse an ecosystem for tech talent to share perspectives, experiences and to learn from each other and this will build the vibrancy of the tech community here in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: MNCs and Local Large Enterprises (LLEs) can play a bigger role in developing digital and tech talent in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: How can we encourage these companies to incubate smaller companies and workers to develop digital/tech talent?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: These companies have the talent development programme as well as expertise to provide learning and the business environment to build and to scale digital capabilities and I believe that these companies can play a very big role in building a bigger pool of talent base than they need and they should play that role.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Many SMEs have taken advantage of these grants.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Yet, there are still many SMEs which have not started down the digitalisation path in a meaningful way.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: But for a digital transformation to be sustainable, it is not enough to adopt some digital solutions.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Yet, we often hear that Singaporeans who work in SMEs find that they have fewer opportunities to acquire these new digital skills, compared to their peers working in LLEs and MNCs.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: What more can the Government do to encourage the long tail of SMEs to reskill and upskill their employees now in order to capture opportunities in the digital economy in a sustainable way?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: How can this reskilling be done at scale?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: How can larger enterprises and TACs support the SME base?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: And how can we encourage and ensure that employees, in particular, who do not invest in such reskilling can go after those opportunities on their own, given that they have more limited resources to do this on their own and may not get the opportunity to put these skills to work in their day jobs?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: Some shared that they need technical expertise, so that they can conduct research and product development here.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: Others shared that they set up their International or Regional Headquarters in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: For these firms, they need not only technical talents but also market expertise.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: For instance, a large software service firm told me that they need talents well-versed in Vietnam and Indonesia to serve the markets there from here.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: The concern is that if firms like this cannot hire or access these talents in Singapore, then they may be compelled to move certain departments or wholly out of Singapore and leave Singaporeans and Singapore for the worse.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: Our people will lose jobs and opportunities to learn from some of the best around the world.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: To this end, I would like to share some thoughts, observations and suggestions.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: First, continue building up our local talents from young.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: Many Singaporeans recognise the value and potential of having tech skills, with parents sending their children to coding and robotics classes and mainstream schools offering coding as an "enrichment" for all upper Primary students.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: This is a good start, but we should build on the momentum and consider introducing computer language as, perhaps, a second language in schools, as well as introducing key concepts and uses of new technology in class.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: The idea is not so much to train everyone to become coding experts, but to inculcate an intuitive understanding of the logic and applications.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: We also need to enhance the global quotient of our young.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: Expand existing in‐market programmes, such as the Singapore‐China Youth Interns Exchange Scheme (YES) and Asia-Ready Exposure Programme (AEP), and actively push our students to take full advantage of these programmes.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: We need to ensure steady growth of a skilled and versatile Singaporean Core.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: I am aware that there are efforts to encourage our young to choose STEM courses and majors; this helps to increase supply to meet the talent demand.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: At the same time, we need to recognise that not all tech firms or tech‐related jobs need hard tech skills.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: A local tech leader told me that she met a Polytechnic graduate who studied tech but decided to become a barista because she did not like coding.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: While there is nothing wrong in choosing a different career, the tech leader wondered if the outcome would have been different if the young barista realised that there was a wide range of options for a career in tech.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: While the public and private sectors could do more to increase awareness on the wide range of career options and groom local talents, the Government could also identify specific skills in demand but lacking in Singapore and co‐sponsor scholarships with companies to train local talents from young.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: Some of the more progressive tech firms are shifting from pure competition or working solo to partnerships.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: Could we, therefore, put in place a support system for skilled gig workers who are trained and well-versed in different operating systems and software, so that they form a formidable talent pool for companies here to tap on?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: And we also need to continue to be open to good global talents who can and want to contribute.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: They fill manpower gaps, but are also good people to exchange knowledge, skills and ideas with so that we can grow together.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: And the third point is on having more role models.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: Healthy diversity is beneficial to boosting talent supply and business outcomes.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: Therefore, we must continue to promote girls and women in tech.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: Similarly, we need more stories of successful Singaporean tech leaders who could be role models to inspire more to join their ranks.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: Could the Government share whether it actively keeps a record of Singaporeans in tech leadership positions in Singapore and overseas?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: Could the Government share their stories and invite them to provide mentorship through the likes of the Singapore Global Executive Programme?

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan
text: Chairman, the digital economy allows us to transcend our geographical constraints and create value for the world.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan
text: Our digital capabilities must become a strategic competitive advantage for us.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan
text: We cannot stop, for competition will not stop.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan
text: And, indeed, we have to go even faster and further, as competition will only accelerate.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan
text: In this regard, what are MCI's strategies to build up an ICT workforce in Singapore with deep expertise and with ever more and exciting opportunities for Singaporeans?

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan
text: More broadly, what are MCI's plans to nurture a digitally-enabled workforce at large that can access opportunities brought about by digital technologies across the economy?

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan
text: At the ecosystem level, how is MCI driving investments in new technologies and their translation into applications to enhance Singapore's long‐term competitive advantage?

speaker: The Chairman
text: Ms Jessica Tan, you can take both cuts.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: Even before the COVID-19 pandemic, workplaces were starting to transform to leverage technology to enable virtual work arrangements.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: If implemented effectively, digital workplaces, including a hybrid of physical and virtual work arrangements, can benefit from increased productivity and improved business results.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: But to realise the opportunities and benefits of the digital workplace, it will require the workforce to be proficient with new skills.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: This is not about developing deep tech skills but rather how to use with confidence new and ever-changing technologies to be able to do their work.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: The ability of the workforce to effectively use virtual and cloud technology, analytics and social and augmented reality tools will enable workers to do their work more effectively, faster and enable them to better communicate their ideas.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: With the pace of digitalisation, how we work, live and play is increasingly digital.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: Hence, trusted, secure and resilient digital architecture and technologies are essential for Singapore and Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: As we invest in future technologies for increased access and speed, we need to also invest to strengthen our digital infrastructures to address unexpected surges in demand against cyber security risks, as well as threats to the resilience of our digital infrastructures.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: Cyber security risks will compromise data security and threaten access and availability of services.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: To sustain our digital economy and way of life, how can Singapore ensure safe and reliable use of such infrastructures and technologies?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: How are our digital infrastructures able to minimise the impact of disruptions to enable businesses to continue to operate and with more digital transactions and operations, business critical information and personal information are exchanged?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: How are we strengthening the security of our digital infrastructures in Singapore to protect our data?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: Our Government continues to invest heavily and our 5G network deployment is well underway.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: But even as we do so, other countries are not idling.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: Given the borderless nature of the digital space and digital threats, it is not enough to rely on domestic levers and programmes to protect Singapore's cyberspace.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: Moreover, as critical infrastructures are very much interlinked and, as countries and markets become increasingly connected digitally, we have become highly vulnerable to disruptions and exploitations by malicious cyber activities.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Mr Chairman, I thank Members for their questions and interest.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Earlier in the Committee of Supply (COS) debate, I updated Members about the progress of our Smart Nation initiative.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Digital technologies are very much a part of our daily lives.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: They have brought day-to-day conveniences, new and improved jobs for our people, and growth opportunities for our businesses.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: But a digital future can be daunting as well.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Enterprises struggle to get the right technologies and talents.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Parents are concerned about the impact on their children.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Our mission is to ensure our people can reap the benefits and rewards of technology, while safeguarding our safety and security.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Our vision of Singapore's digital future is one that is economically vibrant, socially stable and cyber-secure.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: MCI's theme for this year's Committee of Supply is "Building a Vibrant and Secure Digital Future Together".

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The economic opportunities of the digital domain have brought about tremendous transformation and growth in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The positive impact on the wider economy is evident.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Senior Minister of State Janil Puthucheary and Minister of State Tan Kiat How will say more about these later.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This dynamism is equally evident in our society.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Parliamentary Secretary Rahayu Mahzam will provide an update on our efforts to promote digital empowerment and wellness.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: To harness the full potential of the digital domain, I will focus on two aspects of growing importance.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: First, how we will enhance regulations in the digital domain to better protect ourselves and our loved ones, and to strengthen digital security and resilience.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Second, how we will sustain and deepen engagement of every Singaporean in the digital era, to preserve and enhance social cohesion.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Clearly, using technology alone is not enough; it is only half the story.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We also need to better protect ourselves and our loved ones from its risks and threats.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: MCI has three priorities to govern and secure our digital spaces.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The first is to better protect Singaporeans from harmful online content, especially the young and vulnerable.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: A recent Straits Times survey found that among children aged seven to nine, two-thirds use a smartphone daily, and, yet, a third of the parents do not know who their children interact with on social media.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Last year, a National Youth Council poll found that two-thirds of youths had experienced online harms, such as harassment and unwanted advances.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Many developed distrust towards others and experienced stress and anxiety.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Last year, a 10-year-old Italian girl lost her life while participating in an online "Hanging Challenge".

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Users were encouraged to choke themselves until they passed out while live-streaming on TikTok.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Harm can be caused not only to children.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In 2019, social media companies struggled to remove reshares of the video showing a gunman firing on Muslims in a New Zealand mosque.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In 2021, rioters who stormed Capitol Hill in the US used social media to organise and amplify their messages.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Governments worldwide have responded to online harms with new laws.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In 2017, Germany enacted its Network Enforcement Act, which requires platforms to act on unlawful content reported by users.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Last July, Australia enacted an Online Safety Act, which introduces basic safety expectations for online service providers.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The UK's draft Online Safety Bill will create a duty of care for online platforms towards their users, including requirements to take action against harmful content.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Dr Shahira Abdullah, Ms Tin Pei Ling, Dr Wan Rizal and Mr Don Wee are right to ask what more can be done in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Internet content providers must comply with the Internet Code of Practice.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: IMDA has powers to take down content that goes against "public interest, public morality, public order and national harmony".

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: IMDA can also direct Internet Service Providers to block access to prohibited websites.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: To manage children's access to websites and online services, IMDA requires Internet Service Providers to offer filtering services for parents to subscribe to.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: To reduce exposure to age-inappropriate entertainment content, over-the-top and video-on-demand streaming services with content rated NC16 or higher must provide parental controls.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In a 2020 study of online safety for children in 30 countries, international think-tank DQ Institute ranked Singapore fourth.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: But with the growing risks of online harms, we must step up efforts to keep online spaces safe, especially for our children.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Online platforms accessible by users in Singapore can and must take greater responsibility for user safety.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: They should endeavour to keep online spaces free from harmful content, including age-inappropriate content, such as violent and graphic content, and content that promotes sexual violence.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: These include content filters for child accounts and mechanisms for parents to supervise and guide their children online.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Last year, MCI formed the Sunlight Alliance for Action to tackle online harms.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Members of the Alliance want Internet platforms to be diligent in assessing flagged content and remove harmful content without delay.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: But many social media platforms tell us that they cannot be fully aware of all the content that needs moderation.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Much of it is user-generated and the quantity, voluminous.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: User reporting is, therefore, an important way to close the awareness gap and promote prompt follow-up action.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: It will require platforms to set up easy-to-access mechanisms for users to report harmful content, to be responsive in evaluating and acting on these reports and to apprise their users in a timely manner of the actions taken.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This will empower users to highlight harmful content they come across and prevent further spread.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: It will require platforms to provide information on what they are doing to keep users safe.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This includes the prevalence of harmful online content on their platforms, the user reports they have received and acted upon, and the systems and processes they have in place to address harmful online content.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Users can then compare the approaches taken by platforms and make informed decisions about which to engage or disengage.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: They will require relevant online platforms to take more actions to create a safer online environment.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We will study how the Codes can be effectively enforced, including through appropriate legislative updates.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We are also working with MHA to provide Singaporeans with more protection from illegal activities carried out online.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This includes strengthening our levers to tackle online scams, as well as a broader suite of criminal activities taking place online, such as child pornography, terrorism and content that incites violence.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: MCI has frequent engagements with our international and industry partners on issues relating to user safety.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We will continue to consult extensively as we develop these new Codes.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: But the evolving nature of the digital domain will always test the way we design our regulations, as pointed out by Ms Tin Pei Ling.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We need to be clear and unambiguous to uphold security and trust, while not being overly prescriptive or stifling innovation.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The scope of coverage must be wide enough without being excessively expansive.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Simplicity must not be achieved at the expense of effectiveness.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In many ways, our regulatory approach for the digital domain will be similar to how technology services are launched these days, as Minimum Viable Products that will be improved iteratively.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Put another way, perfect must not become the enemy of good.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Instead, we must be prepared to regularly update these Codes, introduce new ones or streamline outdated ones, to deal with emerging issues and new technologies.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Only by doing so can we harness the rich potential of exciting new technologies while guarding against their attendant risks.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Mr Chairman, another important priority of MCI is to strengthen our cybersecurity.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Mr Shawn Huang, Ms Hany Soh and Mr Xie Yao Quan asked what more we are doing to guard against cyber threats.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Since 2018, the Cybersecurity Act has provided a legal framework for CSA to oversee and maintain our national cybersecurity.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The Act is currently focused on securing and protecting our Critical Information Infrastructure.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: These computer systems deliver essential services in the physical world, such as water and power.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Singapore is gravely concerned over the cyberattacks against Ukraine's government websites and national banks.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: It illustrates how essential services can be disrupted remotely and quite easily.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Singapore may be geographically distant from the theatre of action.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: But we cannot disregard the potential knock-on effects arriving on our shores.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This is why, earlier this week, we advised local organisations to beef up their cybersecurity posture.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: But even before the current situation in Ukraine, cyber threats have become more prevalent.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: As our digital realm expands, so, too, the threat surface.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The scale and impact of such attacks elsewhere have also become more serious.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Attacks on systems that run physical infrastructure, such as energy grids and fuel pipelines, have real, tangible impact.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: To strengthen our defences, we need to address three key questions.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: First, how do we raise our situational awareness over Singapore's cyberspace?

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Attackers are constantly on the lookout for serious vulnerabilities, like burglars looking for faulty locks and open windows.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: CSA must, in some way, do the same, but for a very different reason – so that we can advise people to fix their faulty locks and close their windows quickly.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In cyberspace, this means to patch known software vulnerabilities, before malicious actors compromise our systems and steal our data.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Second, what should be considered as Critical Information Infrastructure, or CII?

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The Act currently recognises physical networks and systems as CII.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We need to ensure these virtual assets are properly protected, too, including those that may not be hosted in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Third, how do we secure important digital infrastructure and services beyond CIIs?

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Digital infrastructure and services are the backbone of our connectivity, computing and data storage needs.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: If disrupted or compromised, there could be serious knock-on effects.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Imagine the chaos of not having access to emails, websites and apps.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Mr Chairman, Mr Sharael Taha asked how we could enable businesses to innovate and grow while safeguarding consumers and their personal data.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Data is a critical resource for the digital economy.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In 2012, we enacted the Personal Data Protection Act, or PDPA.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: It strikes a careful balance between allowing organisations to harness data for innovation and growth and ensuring proper safeguards and accountability.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In 2020, to adapt to the evolving digital landscape, we amended the PDPA.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Among several amendments, we explicitly recognised business improvement as a legitimate use of data.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Close to 90% of businesses agreed that the PDPA helped them prepare for the digital economy.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: More than 80% of consumers said that the PDPA helped them trust that their personal data is protected from misuse by organisations.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: As a result of the pandemic-induced economic uncertainty, the implementation of the new penalties was temporarily held back.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We will also strengthen safeguards in other areas.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Currently, consumers and small businesses try to resolve contractual disputes with their telco, or media service providers, directly or through existing dispute resolution options.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: To supplement these options, IMDA will launch an Alternative Dispute Resolution (ADR) Scheme which is designed to be affordable and effective.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: When a case is brought to the ADR, it will be mandatory for the service providers to participate in the resolution process.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: From April, this will provide a new helpful channel to resolve such disputes.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Mr Chairman, the three priorities I have described to govern and secure our digital spaces will form the building blocks of a vibrant and secure digital future.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: But, Sir, technology has also changed the way we interact with one another, our communities and the world.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The global media and information landscape have become more diffused, with competing narratives and echo chambers, and more news sources than anyone can keep up with.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Mr Don Wee rightly pointed out the need for trusted information sources and genuine engagement and a holistic approach to target the spread of misinformation.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Indeed, these have been critical in combating the COVID-19 pandemic.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We could not have handled a public health crisis if the public did not trust the health authorities or did not believe the information they were receiving.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: That is precisely why, from the very outset, we resolved to keep the public informed as fully and expeditiously as possible.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We were determined to tell it as it is, never fudge or sugarcoat, never hide.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: As the Prime Minister observed recently, if we had been a low-trust society, people would not have understood the need for safe management measures (SMMs) or abided by them.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Our infection rates would be higher, far fewer people would be vaccinated, and many more people would have died.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: To preserve this trust, we must also have appropriate laws.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The COVID-19 pandemic has, therefore, underlined the crucial importance of retaining public trust and maintaining trusted sources of information.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: MCI has done this by expanding and refreshing our communications channels and launching targeted campaigns like VacciNationSG to support our vaccination drive.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Gov.sg's 10 platforms have close to two million more subscribers, compared to before the pandemic.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We commissioned e-getai shows for seniors that received over 7.5 million views and catchy music videos with over nine million views online.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: To better engage Singaporeans from all walks of life and understand their concerns, REACH expanded its digital outreach through e-Listening Points and virtual dialogues.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In 2021, more than 70,000 Singaporeans contributed feedback to REACH, up from 59,000 in 2020.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Through these concerted efforts, polls show that three in four members of the public think that the Government has provided sufficient information on COVID-19 in recent months.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Over 86% agreed that these messages helped in their decision to get vaccinated.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: It is critical that we maintain these high levels of trust as we strive to bounce back from the COVID-19 pandemic and see through future crises as Singapore Together.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Our local media companies play an important role in this mission to inform and engage our citizens.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: They help to keep Singaporeans united by providing a Singapore lens through which citizens can make sense of global events; presenting an authoritative source of information that cuts through the noise of an online space chock-full of clickbait content and misinformation; and producing content in our official languages that celebrates our diverse culture and creates shared experiences for all Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Clearly, our local media companies serve a broader mission beyond commercial success.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This is why the Government put our support behind SPH Media Trust.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We have explained the background extensively during the Parliament Sittings in May 2021 and February 2022, but I will reiterate two key points.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: First, our local media, like media outlets across the world, have seen their advertising and subscription revenue drastically reduced, buffeted by the rise of digital content platforms and new avenues for free content.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We hope they can become self-sustaining, but it remains to be seen whether or when this can happen.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Mr Leong Mun Wai said SPH is Government-owned.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: If it was, there would be no question today of public funding.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: He then asked if the SPH listed company could be made to contribute more to the new SPH Media Trust.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: If the restructuring proposal involved an even higher contribution, the shareholders could have walked away.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The Company Limited by Guarantee (CLG) might not have been formed and the SPH media business could have remained on its trajectory of decline with scant hope for revival.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In time to come, there would be nothing worthwhile to preserve.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Parliament has been fully briefed on the need for the restructuring and accepted that our local mainstream media is worthy of public funding.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: When compared to the investments seen elsewhere in the world, the amount of funding to support our local media's transformation must be meaningful, in order for their efforts to have a chance to succeed.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: I have also explained in detail how the Government will keep them accountable.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Let us now direct our attention on charting the way forward, such as those highlighted by Ms Hany Soh on how the media can better meet the needs of different demographics.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: For example, Mediacorp is working with their news broadcasters, as well as clan associations to identify new talent to sustain dialect radio news broadcasts.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Mediacorp produces an animation series on sustainability and environmental awareness, so that parents and their children know why this is important and how they can contribute to this national priority.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Left to the free market, such programmes are unlikely to be viable.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: I, therefore, urge Members to give our local media and journalists the fullest support, because they deserve it.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: As the media industry adapts to the rise of digital, exciting new opportunities have also emerged.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Singapore is well-positioned to benefit because of our robust intellectual property and legal frameworks and our role as a connector between markets and cultures.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: (In Mandarin):   For many Singaporeans, Internet access has become a basic necessity, just like water and electricity.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In today's world, building a vibrant and secure digital future is critical for a country's survival and prosperity.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Singapore will continue to face unknown challenges, but we will not give up.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The Government is committed to helping every Singaporean succeed in the digital age through various measures.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: SMEs at all stages of the digital journey will have the opportunity to progress and open up new frontiers, even as they face various pressures.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Workers in various sectors will have the opportunity to deepen their skills.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Everyone will receive support to level up their digital skills and improve their livelihoods.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Seniors will have the opportunity to embrace lifelong learning, so that they master technology and maintain social ties.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Children will be better protected from undesirable content and online harms.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We are also working hard to strengthen the security of our digital infrastructure to boost our people's and businesses' confidence in the digital future.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Mr Chairman, let me first start by thanking Members for their questions and interest in MCI's work.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: I will elaborate on MCI's plans to build a society which continues to be inclusive, relevant and prepared for a digital future.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: As Minister Josephine Teo mentioned, digital technologies are very much a part of our daily lives.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Going digital has opened numerous possibilities – from facilitating daily interactions with family and friends to engendering new conveniences in many aspects of our lives.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: This is why digital access and meaningful engagement with technologies have become key to our quality of life today.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: MCI will continue strengthening digital literacy and wellness, by working closely with community partners and volunteers to achieve three key goals.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: First, digital access and digital adoption for all; next, learning and mastery of digital skills, for all to seize new opportunities in the digital economy; and equally important, for our people to be equipped to recognise and respond to dangers online.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: To ensure that Singaporeans, regardless of age, background or skill level are empowered to take charge of their own digital future, our first goal of digital access and adoption is a basic good that everyone should have, comprising Internet connectivity, tech devices and the ability to make use of them.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: I recognise that this is an issue close to the hearts of many Members, including Senior Parliamentary Secretary Baey Yam Keng, Mr Seah Kian Peng, Mr Sharael Taha and Ms Hany Soh.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Our broadband connectivity and basic devices are important to our people.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Still, we recognise that every Singaporean must have this access.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Today, we have digital access programmes, such as NEU PC Plus and Home Access.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Almost double the number, as compared to those assisted before the pandemic.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Moving forward, we are looking to enhance our digital access programmes to reach more low-income households and help them more conveniently receive affordable digital access.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: This will include working with MSF and social service organisations to engage and assist low-income households in their applications.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Having ensured that our people have access to the digital realm, we also look at addressing the needs of particular segments of individuals and businesses so that they can adopt – that is, to use and benefit from – digital.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Mr Sharael Taha highlighted that there may be some in the community who are less familiar with the digital space, including seniors and some hawkers.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: At the height of the pandemic, the SG Digital Office (SDO) was set up to engage precisely these groups that may need additional and tailored support.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
